original_question: Consider the same hard-core lattice-gas setting as in Conjecture 2.1, but restricted to non-regular trees with all fugacities equal. Can one prove the Conjecture 2.1 uniqueness claim in that tree setting?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Conjecture 2.1 together with the immediately following remark that says the conjecture is still open even for a non-regular tree with all fugacities equal.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the hard-core lattice-gas part of the paper, the uniqueness side of Conjecture 2.1, and the exact special case that Sokal explicitly singles out right after the conjecture: non-regular trees with equal fugacities.
missing_details: The paper's setting is a countably infinite graph; in the tree specialization, the tree should be stated to be countably infinite.
The conjecture is parameterized by the maximum degree Δ, so the question should specify a non-regular tree T of bounded maximum degree Δ.
The model should be stated explicitly as the nearest-neighbor hard-core lattice gas on T, equivalently independent sets with finite-volume weight proportional to λ^{|I|}.
Equal fugacities should be written explicitly as w_x = λ for every vertex x, with λ >= 0.
The phrase 'uniqueness claim' should be made precise as uniqueness of the infinite-volume Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle Gibbs measure.
The exact Conjecture 2.1 threshold is missing: in the equal-fugacity specialization the intended bound is λ < ((Δ-1)^(Δ-1))/((Δ-2)^Δ).
Sokal's actual multivariate phrasing is uniform: all fugacities are bounded by some constant c strictly below that threshold; the equal-fugacity version is the specialization w_x ≡ λ.
The parenthetical strengthening in Conjecture 2.1 is omitted: Sokal also asks whether the same statement might remain true at the endpoint λ = ((Δ-1)^(Δ-1))/((Δ-2)^Δ).
The intended regime is Δ >= 3; this is the regime in which the regular-tree threshold formula is meaningful.

To be fully paper-faithful, the question should make clear that it asks only for this tree-specialized case of Conjecture 2.1, not for broader statements about nonuniqueness, high-fugacity phases, or zero-free regions.
No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree-of-polynomial, or nilpotency assumptions are relevant here; the missing stand-alone data are graph-theoretic and Gibbs-measure-theoretic.
refined_question: Let T = (V,E) be a countably infinite non-regular tree of maximum degree Δ >= 3. Consider the nearest-neighbor hard-core lattice gas on T with uniform fugacity λ >= 0, so that finite-volume configurations are independent sets I weighted proportionally to λ^{|I|}. Can one prove that the associated infinite-volume Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle Gibbs measure is unique for every λ < ((Δ-1)^(Δ-1))/((Δ-2)^Δ), thereby establishing the non-regular-tree, equal-fugacity special case explicitly singled out after Conjecture 2.1? (As in Sokal's parenthetical comment in Conjecture 2.1, one may also ask whether uniqueness could persist at the endpoint λ = ((Δ-1)^(Δ-1))/((Δ-2)^Δ).)
justification: Your draft is aimed at the right target, but it is not yet fully stand-alone. In Section 2, Sokal first defines the hard-core lattice gas via the independent-set partition function and then states Conjecture 2.1 as a max-degree uniqueness conjecture for countably infinite graphs. Immediately afterward, he observes that even the special case of a non-regular tree with equal fugacities appears to be open. That observation, rather than a broader neighboring problem, is exactly what your draft is trying to capture. The refined version therefore adds the missing ingredients that the paper treats as implicit: countable infinitude, maximum degree Δ, equal fugacity notation, the DLR meaning of uniqueness, and the precise regular-tree threshold that motivates Conjecture 2.1. No algebraic ambient-ring or homogeneity conditions are relevant in this paper.
